# Tone Voice and Localization Rules

This page compiles tone, voice, and localization rules for Simpro messaging.

## Voice Baseline

Simpro writing should be clear, practical, confident, trade-aware, human, outcome-oriented, and evidence-backed. It should avoid vague software claims, inflated AI language, and unsupported ROI language.

## Named-Author Blog Treatment

- Named-author Simpro blogs and thought leadership may use first-person judgment, contractions, operational scenes, decisive opinions, and short punchlines.
- Author opinion must remain distinguishable from empirical fact.
- Metrics, market comparisons, product status, roadmap statements, and commercial claims remain proof gated.
- Em dashes are prohibited. Use a period, comma, colon, or parentheses when the grammar supports it.
- Product pages and landing pages retain their existing restrained channel treatment.

## Localization Rules

- Localize spelling, terminology, currency, market examples, and regulatory references.
- Do not localize the core positioning into a different category claim.
- Do not change proof status, metric wording, or customer outcome context when adapting copy by market.
- Keep region-specific claims tied to region-specific source material.

## Drafting Checks

- Does the copy state who the audience is?
- Does the copy connect the feature to a source-supported operational or business outcome?
- Does the copy avoid unsupported metrics or customer outcomes?
- Does the copy preserve approved Lightning naming and architecture when AI features are involved?

1. Trade Snapshot & Geographic Scope
Trade Overview
Electrical contracting businesses install, maintain, test, and repair electrical systems across commercial, industrial, and residential properties. Most firms operate with a licensed field workforce — electricians, apprentices, and, in commercial settings, project supervisors — supported by an office team handling quoting, scheduling, compliance documentation, and administration. Commercial work is the primary content lens for this profile — including fitouts, switchboard upgrades, test and compliance services, and maintenance contracts — with residential included as a meaningful secondary lens, particularly for smaller operators who blend the two.
Geographic Scope

North America (US) — Large, fragmented market. Commercial and industrial electrical services dominate among growth-stage businesses — data/comms fitouts, switchboard and panel upgrades, high-voltage work, fire alarm and security integration. Contractor licensing is state- and province-level (Master Electrician, Journeyman). Many firms serve both residential and commercial markets. NEC compliance and AHJ permit requirements are central to project delivery. Accounting integrations (QuickBooks) and mobile-first workflows are primary technology requirements for this region.
United Kingdom — Established contractor market with a strong compliance culture. Domestic Installer and commercial electrician segments operate under NICEIC or NAPIT certification. EICRs (Electrical Installation Condition Reports) are mandatory deliverables across the commercial and landlord sectors. Contract maintenance and test and inspection work are common revenue streams for mid-sized businesses. 'Engineer' is standard terminology for commercial roles; 'electrician' is the trade self-description. Accounting integration is predominantly with Xero.
Australia & New Zealand — Strong tradie culture with growing solar PV, EV charging, and smart electrical segments. Contractors operate under state and territory licensing regimes and AS/NZS 3000 Wiring Rules. Certificate of Compliance for Electrical Work (CCEW) is issued after every qualifying job in most states. Commercial fitout and maintenance contracts are common for growth-stage businesses. 'Switchboard' replaces 'panel' in local terminology. Xero is the dominant accounting platform.

2. Target Business Profile
Overall Company Size Range
Typically 2–80 employees, encompassing licensed electricians, apprentices, and administrative or office staff. The platform sweet spot is 5–50 employees. Larger firms (80–150+) are present but represent a smaller proportion of the ICP for this trade; their complexity often requires deeper project management and multi-site capabilities.
Dominant Business Maturity (Archetype)
Blended Empower and Elevate. The majority of incoming buyers are moving off manual processes (spreadsheets, whiteboards, paper job cards) or have outgrown entry-level FSM tools such as Tradify, ServiceM8, or Jobber. Elevate-stage businesses are scaling and encountering operational friction — scheduling complexity, poor job costing visibility, and administrative load that can no longer be absorbed by the current team. Excel-stage businesses (data-driven, using platforms for forecasting and margin optimisation) are present but less common in this vertical. [Hindsight-augmented]
Size Segments
Segment A: Smaller Operator
1–10 employees, often an owner-operator with 2–6 electricians. Primarily residential and small commercial call-out work — fault-finding, outlet additions, consumer unit replacements, small fitouts. Strong urgency around quoting speed, mobile-first job management, and getting paid faster. Technology maturity is basic: phone, WhatsApp, spreadsheet, or a lightweight app like Tradify or Jobber. The owner is both the economic buyer and the primary user of the platform. Concerns centre on whether the product is 'too much' for their size and whether implementation will disrupt operations. [Hindsight-augmented]
Segment B: Growth-Stage Business
10–60 employees. A blend of service call-outs, multi-year maintenance contracts, and commercial project work. Beginning to manage compliance documentation at scale, asset registers, contract billing, and multi-crew scheduling. Needs integrated job costing, reporting for owner financial visibility, and the ability to invoice against project milestones. Technology maturity is intermediate — existing FSM tool (ServiceM8, Tradify, Fergus, or similar) that the business has outgrown. Operations Manager or Service Manager may initiate the evaluation, but the owner retains sign-off authority and ROI clarity is the primary closing requirement. [Hindsight-augmented]
Shared Characteristics Across Sizes

Job types span service calls, test and inspection, maintenance contracts, and fitout or installation projects
Material tracking and job costing are persistent pain points regardless of business size
Compliance documentation (test certificates, EICRs, certificates of compliance) is non-negotiable at every scale
Owner or principal is typically the economic buyer and final decision-maker [Hindsight-augmented]
Mobile-first field workforce — electricians in the field are a primary user group for any platform

Buyer Dynamics & Decision Intelligence

Primary Decision Maker — Owner, Director, or Managing Director. At larger Growth-Stage businesses, an Operations Manager or General Manager may lead the evaluation but the owner retains commercial sign-off authority and typically makes the final decision. [Hindsight-augmented]
Key Influencers — Office Manager or Service Coordinator (scheduling, admin, quoting workflows); Finance Manager or bookkeeper (payment velocity, Xero/QuickBooks integration, invoicing accuracy); Senior Electrician or Field Supervisor (mobile usability, job documentation on site).
Decision Frame — ROI clarity combined with confidence that implementation is manageable. Buyers compare against their current manual processes or entry-level tools (Tradify, ServiceM8, Jobber). They want proof the platform pays for itself quickly and will not create disruption during rollout. The most common objection is not cost — it is complexity and change-management anxiety. When buyers do choose a platform, the dominant purchase frame is 'one system for everything' — service calls, projects, and contracts — rather than a feature-specific evaluation. [Hindsight-augmented]
Buying Urgency Triggers — Growth strain on manual processes; missed invoices or consistently slow payment cycles; a lost contract due to poor compliance documentation; failed compliance audit or inspection; staff frustration or departure creating process vulnerability; owner being pulled back into admin instead of sales or supervision; integration pain with accounting and quoting tools — double-entry between Xero/QuickBooks and spreadsheets or a lightweight FSM reaching a visible breaking point. [Hindsight-augmented]
Technology Maturity Context — Most incoming buyers are at Empower or early Elevate. They are migrating from spreadsheets plus Tradify, ServiceM8, or Jobber combinations. Deep technical integration requirements are uncommon; Xero or QuickBooks integration and mobile app usability are the primary technology requirements. Buyers in this trade have low tolerance for long or complex implementation cycles — phased rollout framing is important**. [Hindsight-augmented]**

3. Common Job Types & Work Scope
Work Types & Real-World Examples
Installation

New switchboard (ANZ) / consumer unit (UK) / service panel (NA) installations
Power outlet and circuit additions; sub-main upgrades
Commercial fitouts — lighting, power distribution, data and communications cabling, access control
New residential builds and extensions (NA and ANZ); domestic rewires (UK)
EV charger installation — growing commercial and residential segment across all regions
Solar PV system installation and grid connection (primary in ANZ, growing in NA and UK)
Fire alarm, emergency lighting, and security system installation

Inspection & Testing

Electrical Installation Condition Reports (EICRs) — UK commercial and landlord sector
Certificate of Compliance for Electrical Work (CCEW) issued after every qualifying job in ANZ
Periodic inspection and testing under AS/NZS 3000 / BS 7671 / NEC
Pre-purchase property electrical inspections
Arc flash hazard assessments (NA, commercial and industrial)
PAT testing (UK); thermal imaging and switchboard inspections

Maintenance

Scheduled preventive maintenance on switchboards, distribution boards, and lighting systems under service contracts
Annual or periodic compliance checks for commercial tenants, landlords, and facilities clients
Emergency lighting system testing and certification
Energy management and monitoring system maintenance
PPM (planned preventive maintenance) contracts — typically monthly, quarterly, or annual cadence; compliance documentation delivery is a key client expectation

Repair & Fault-Finding

Emergency call-outs for power failures, tripped circuits, or faulty equipment
Fault diagnosis for commercial and industrial plant and switchgear
Consumer unit, switchboard, and distribution board fault rectification
Lighting, emergency system, and access control fault repair

Work Scope & Job Shape
Small Jobs / Call-Outs
Single-electrician or two-person call-outs for fault rectification, outlet additions, minor switchboard work, or quick commercial requests. Typically 1–4 hours. Rapid quote-to-invoice cycle is critical — same-day or next-day invoicing is the expectation. Materials often sourced on the day with limited pre-job planning.
Recurring Contracts
Monthly, quarterly, or annual maintenance agreements with commercial property owners, facilities managers, or tenants. Compliance documentation delivery (certificates, test results, service reports) is a key contractual obligation. Contract billing, visit scheduling, and renewal visibility are important operational requirements at this scale.
Mid-Sized Projects
Commercial fitouts, switchboard replacements, and multi-phase electrical installation projects spanning 2–16 weeks. Often involve phased billing milestones and coordination with other trades (plumbing, HVAC, data contractors). Variation orders and material uplift are common and frequently go untracked, creating margin leakage. Asset handover documentation is required at project completion.
4. Operational Challenges by Role
Owner / Business Leader

No real-time view of job profitability on active projects — margins are only understood after invoicing, often too late to course-correct on labour overruns or material cost blow-outs. [Hindsight-augmented]
Quoting is done from memory, past invoices, or spreadsheets — resulting in inconsistent pricing, insufficient margin for complexity, and no systematic review of job performance against quote.
Growth creates invisible operational drag — more jobs, more crews, more compliance obligations, but no proportional increase in financial clarity or management confidence.
Compliance exposure is a liability risk: if test certificates, EICRs, or certificates of compliance are not delivered consistently, contracts can be lost or professional indemnity claims can follow.
Cannot scale without adding office headcount — administrative burden grows faster than revenue because manual coordination is the only option. [Hindsight-augmented]
Difficult to identify which job types, clients, or contract types are genuinely profitable — mix decisions are made by feel.

Office / Back-Office Staff

Scheduling is manual and reactive — tracking which electrician is available, geographically close, and holds the right licence or certification for a job requires constant phone and messaging coordination. [Hindsight-augmented]
Quoting is time-consuming due to variable materials pricing, labour rates by qualification level, and compliance requirements — each quote is rebuilt from scratch.
Job completion information (timesheets, materials used, site notes, test results) arrives late, incompletely, or not at all from the field — creating invoicing delays and disputes.
Invoicing requires manual data reconciliation across timesheets, delivery dockets, and field notes rather than pulling from a single job record.
Purchase order and materials management is ad-hoc — leading to stock-outs, over-ordering, or missed material charges on invoices.
Maintaining compliance document registers (certificates, EICRs, test records) manually is time-consuming and error-prone at scale.

Field Technician

Arriving on site without full job history, previous test results, asset details, or clear scope — leading to avoidable delays, incorrect materials, and repeat visits. [Hindsight-augmented]
Timesheets and material usage tracked on paper or via text message, creating inaccuracies in job costing and leaving billable time off invoices.
No formal mechanism to capture variation work or additional materials on-site — extra work is performed but not charged.
Compliance documentation (test certificates, circuit schedules) completed after the fact from memory, increasing error risk and creating liability exposure if records are challenged.
Field technicians cannot see real-time schedule changes, updated job briefs, or purchase approvals without calling the office — creating repeated interruptions and delays.

Finance

Invoice approval delays on project and contract work — compliance certificates and client sign-offs must be in place before payment is released, and chasing these is manual. [Hindsight-augmented]
AR ageing pressure from slow follow-up on service and call-out invoices — particularly for businesses invoicing weekly or monthly in arrears.
No real-time view of WIP (work in progress) value against outstanding invoices — cash flow position is unclear until end-of-month close.
Materials costs entered late or inconsistently, making job-level margin analysis unreliable and hindering any meaningful financial review.

5. Profitability Pressure Points
Revenue Leakage

Variation work captured verbally on-site but never formally quoted or invoiced — extra circuits, material upgrades, or scope additions that never become billable revenue. [Hindsight-augmented]
Billable travel time and first-hour call-out fees missed due to informal or absent job tracking.
Test and inspection work completed without generating a compliance certificate or accompanying invoice — service delivered but not charged.
Materials used on-site not reconciled against purchase orders — unbilled material charges reduce gross margin on individual jobs across the portfolio.
Deposits not collected upfront on materials-heavy jobs — cash tied up in materials before any revenue is recovered.

Margin Erosion

Return visits caused by incomplete site information — wrong specification, missing test results, or incorrect materials loaded — add unbilled labour and vehicle costs to jobs without corresponding revenue. [Hindsight-augmented]
Labour overruns on project work not visible until invoicing — by then, cost recovery via re-negotiation or variation is not possible.
Inefficient routing and unoptimised scheduling create unproductive time between jobs, reducing daily technician utilisation and effective hourly rate.
Apprentice and trade assistant hours recorded inconsistently — understated costs inflate apparent margin on jobs and distort business profitability analysis.

Cash Flow Delays

Project invoices held up pending compliance certificates or client sign-off documentation — revenue is earned but not collectible until paperwork is complete. [Hindsight-augmented]
Slow invoicing cycle from job completion to invoice dispatch — in businesses that rely on manual timesheet collection, days or weeks can pass before an invoice is raised.
Variation orders not documented at the time of work — disputes at invoice stage delay payment on otherwise complete jobs.
Materials-heavy jobs proceed without upfront deposits — the business absorbs the cost of materials before being paid.

Limited Financial Visibility

No real-time view of labour costs versus quoted hours on active projects — margin risk is invisible until jobs are closed and reconciled. [Hindsight-augmented]
WIP value not visible during the month — decisions about resourcing, hiring, or taking on new work are made without confidence in the underlying cash position.
Job-level profitability only knowable retrospectively — making it impossible to course-correct on underperforming jobs before they close.
No aggregate view of revenue contribution by work type (call-out vs. contract vs. project) — business mix decisions are made by instinct rather than data.

6. Compliance & Risk Factors
Regulatory & Compliance Drivers

United States / Canada — State and provincial electrical contractor and worker licensing (Master Electrician, Journeyman); National Electrical Code (NEC) compliance and local AHJ permit and inspection requirements; NFPA 70E arc flash and electrical safety standards for commercial and industrial environments; low-voltage licensing (data, comms, security) is separately regulated in many US states.
United Kingdom — BS 7671 18th Edition Wiring Regulations compliance; Part P Building Regulations for domestic electrical work; NICEIC or NAPIT scheme membership for certifying contractors; Electrical Installation Condition Reports (EICRs) as mandatory deliverables for commercial and landlord-owned properties; five-year EICR periodic inspection cycle for commercial tenants and landlord compliance under the Housing Act.
Australia & New Zealand — State and territory-based electrical contractor licensing and electrical worker licensing (varies by state); AS/NZS 3000 Wiring Rules (the Wiring Rules) compliance; Certificate of Compliance for Electrical Work (CCEW) required after every regulated electrical installation in most states; Safe Work Australia and state WHS/OHS legislation for site safety obligations.

Safety & Risk Considerations

Working with live electrical systems creates injury, fire, and property damage risk when work is incomplete, incorrectly documented, or performed by unlicensed or unsupervised personnel.
Arc flash and electrocution risk requires documented risk assessments and appropriate PPE, particularly for switchboard and high-voltage work.
Working at height (luminaire installation, rooftop solar, ceiling-mounted systems) adds physical injury risk requiring Safe Work Method Statements (SWMS) or equivalent.
Unplanned return visits due to incorrect first-visit work increase both safety exposure and customer trust erosion.

Customer Trust & Credibility Signals

Electrical test certificates, inspection reports, and EICRs delivered promptly, correctly, and professionally after every qualifying job.
Compliance documentation available digitally and on demand — critical for commercial property managers and FM clients managing their own compliance obligations.
Crew credentials, licensing details, and insurance documentation visible to commercial clients on larger accounts.
Professional, consistent job cards and completion reports that demonstrate systematic, auditable work practices — particularly important for facilities management and government contracts.

Consequences of Getting It Wrong

Failed inspection or audit requiring costly rework before project sign-off, with potential for voided warranties and delay penalty exposure.
Regulatory penalty, licensing suspension, or scheme membership removal for uncertified or non-compliant work.
Insurance claims voided if compliance documentation is absent, incorrect, or cannot be produced at the time of an incident.
Contract termination or non-renewal from commercial clients whose own regulatory compliance depends on receiving certified electrical documentation from their contractors.

7. Value Pillar Alignment
Confidence in Profitability
Electrical contractors lose margin on projects and service contracts when labour overruns, untracked variation work, and material discrepancies are invisible until after invoicing. Real-time job cost visibility against quoted hours — combined with material tracking from field to office — gives owners the financial clarity to course-correct before a job closes, not after. For businesses running maintenance contracts, profitability confidence depends on knowing which contract sites are performing and which are absorbing disproportionate resource without commensurate revenue. The inability to answer 'is this job making money?' until the job is closed is the defining profitability challenge of this trade. [Hindsight-augmented]
Operational Visibility — Quote to Cash
The electrical trade's quote-to-cash lifecycle spans complex and disconnected touchpoints — rapid call-out quotes, multi-phase project billing with milestone holds, compliance certification requirements before client payment release, and recurring contract administration. Disconnected tools mean delays accumulate at every handoff: quoting done in spreadsheets, scheduling in messaging apps, timesheets on paper, invoicing from incomplete field records. End-to-end visibility from quote acceptance through job execution, certification delivery, and payment closes those gaps and compresses the cash cycle — removing the manual reconciliation layer that slows every invoice. Smarter Field-to-Office Workflows

In electrical businesses, automation removes friction from the highest-volume, lowest-value administrative tasks: invoice generation from completed jobs, compliance certificate dispatch, maintenance schedule triggering from asset records, and accounts receivable follow-up on outstanding invoices. For a business managing dozens of service calls per week or a PPM contract portfolio, automated workflows remove the administrative ceiling that would otherwise require additional headcount to manage. Automation is positioned as an operational enabler for skilled electricians — not a replacement for trade expertise. [Hindsight-augmented]

Against ServiceTitan, the competitive motion is real and winnable — 25 deals, 56.0% win rate. Buyers evaluating for commercial electrical work encounter gaps in project management depth, compliance documentation workflows, and accounting integration flexibility. The loss pattern reveals an integration story clarity gap and a compelling event requirement — both should be pre-empted in the sales process. [Hindsight-augmented]
Against AroFlo in ANZ (where AroFlo is the home market), the competitive dynamic is peer-level — both platforms serve the same ICP. Differentiation should focus on platform depth, project capability, implementation experience, and accounting integration breadth.
Housecall Pro (37.5% win rate) and Fergus (45.0% win rate) are two competitors where current win rates suggest qualification drift or a messaging gap — monitor closely**. [Hindsight-augmented]**
Procore deals are outside the core ICP for this profile — do not build campaign messaging or content around displacement of these platforms in the electrical vertical.

10.7 Objection Handling & Competitive Displacement
Primary Objections by Stage

'It's too complex / too much for us' — Frame implementation as a phased rollout starting with a lean workflow set — quoting, scheduling, mobile, and invoicing in phase one. De-risk by referencing customers of similar size who achieved value quickly (Norberg Electric, Enhanced Electrical Services). The objection is change-management anxiety, not a genuine product-fit concern for businesses in the core ICP. [Hindsight-augmented]
'We don't feel any urgency to change' — Quantify the cost of the status quo: missed variation billing, slow payment cycles, admin hours that could be recovered, and the margin visibility gap on active jobs. Use buyer language from Hindsight win drivers: 'you're running margin blind on every project right now.' [Hindsight-augmented]
'We're worried about the implementation' — Proactively solve for rollout: define a lean phase-one workflow set, confirm local support availability, and set clear time-to-value expectations. Implementation concerns appear in 93 lost deals — pre-empting this objection in the sales process is a direct win-rate lever. [Hindsight-augmented]
Competitive Displacement Intelligence
vs. Tradify / ServiceM8 / Jobber (NA, UK, ANZ) — Acknowledge these tools work well at small scale — then challenge on what they cannot do: job costing visibility, project management, maintenance contract scheduling, integrated BI reporting, and accounting depth. Win rates against these tools (75–86%) confirm the platform wins when the full capability comparison is made. [Hindsight-augmented]
vs. ServiceTitan (NA) — Acknowledge it as a credible platform for high-volume residential dispatch. Then reframe: if their work includes commercial projects, maintenance contracts, or compliance documentation requirements, ServiceTitan is built around a different motion. Ask them to show you how ServiceTitan handles multi-phase project billing, compliance certificate tracking, or Xero integration — those workflow tests reveal the fit gap. Win rate against ServiceTitan is 56% in this vertical; it is consistently winnable when the conversation shifts to commercial workflow fit. [Hindsight-augmented]
vs. Joblogic / Commusoft (UK) — Lead with platform depth, project capability, and local reference customers. Win rate is even at 50% — stronger differentiation narrative needed. Peer references and review strategy are key levers. [Hindsight-augmented]
vs. Fergus (ANZ) — Win rate has softened to 45%. Migration support and implementation confidence are the primary decision levers. Lead with the unified platform story and maintenance planner capability. [Hindsight-augmented]
vs. AroFlo (NA/UK only) — Low win rate (23%) reflects dataset composition — AroFlo is a peer platform in ANZ, not a displacement target there. Do not build NA/UK campaign messaging around this matchup. [Hindsight-augmented]
Sales Conversation Guardrails
Always quantify the ROI case — abstract value propositions stall at the same rate that specific business cases close. Use the prospect's own numbers: crew size, jobs per month, current invoicing cycle. [Hindsight-augmented]
Never generalise integration claims — name Xero and QuickBooks specifically. Vague integration language is a proven loss risk in this vertical. [Hindsight-augmented]
Address implementation concerns before close, not at close — implementation anxiety appears in 93 lost deals and is the primary change-management objection across both segments. [Hindsight-augmented]
Follow-up cadence is a direct win-rate lever — 106 lost deals carry a follow-up cadence driver. Every post-demo touchpoint should add value, not just chase. [Hindsight-augmented]

Proof Gaps

No Simpro UK electrical case study with quantified project or contract billing metrics — needed for UK segment content assets.
AroFlo electrical case study metrics not retrieved at time of v1.0 generation — 9 customers identified, some metrics need to be populated if they become available.
No project-work-specific electrical case study for any brand — a commercial fitout or switchboard project story with margin or billing metrics would close the proof gap for Segment B buyers.
Hindsight dataset reflects NA-weighted deal records — UK and ANZ regional patterns are underrepresented. Regional breakdowns should be added when sufficient deal volume per region is available.
